source_text: –Τί ἀποκριθήσῃτῷ κριτῇ ὁ τοὺς τοίχους ἀμφιεννὺς, ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἐνδύεις; ὁ τοὺς ἵππους κοσμῶν, τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀσχημονοῦντα περιορᾷς; ὁ κατασήπων τὸν σῖτον, τοὺς πεινῶντας οὐ τρέφεις; ὁ τὸν χρυσὸν κατορύσσων, τοῦ ἀγχομένου καταφρονεῖς; Ἐὰν δὲ δὴ καὶ γυνὴ φιλόπλουτος συνοι κεῖ, διπλάσιον ἡ νόσος· τάς τε γὰρ τρυφὰς ἀναφλέγει· καὶ τὰς φιληδονίας συναύξει, καὶ κέντρα ταῖς περιέργοις ἐπιθυμίαις ἐνίησι, λίθους τινὰς ἐπινοοῦσα, μαργαρίτας καὶ σμαράγδους καὶ ὑακίνθους, καὶ χρυσὸν, τὸν μὲν χαλκεύουσα, τὸν δὲ ἐξυφαίνουσα, καὶ διὰ πάσης ἀπειροκαλίας τὴν νόσον αὔξουσα. Οὐ γὰρ ἐκ παρέργου ἡ περὶ ταῦτα σπουδὴ, ἀλλὰ καὶ νύκτες καὶ ἡμέραι τὰς περὶ τούτων μερίμνας ἔχουσι. Καὶ μυρίοι τινὲς κόλακες, ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις αὐτῶν ὑποτρέχοντες, συνάγουσι τοὺς ἀνθοβαφεῖς, τοὺς χρυσοχόους, τοὺς μυρεψοὺς, τοὺς ὑφάντας, τοὺς ποικιλτάς. Οὐδένα χρόνον ἀναπνεῖν δίδωσι τῷ ἀνδρὶ ἐκ τῶν συνεχῶν αὐτῆς ἐπιταγμάτων. Οὐδεὶς ἐξαρκεῖ πλοῦτος ταῖς γυναικείαις ἐπιθυμίαις ὑπηρετούμενος, οὐδ' ἂν ἐκ ποταμῶν ἐπιῤῥέῃ· ὅταν σπουδάζηται μὲν παρ' αὐταῖς τὸ βαρβαρικὸν μύρον, ὡς τὸ ἐξ ἀγορᾶς ἔλαιον, τὰ δὲ ἐκ θαλάττης ἄνθη, ἡ κόχλος, ἡ πίννα, ὑπὲρ τὸ ἐκ τῶν προβάτων ἔριον. Χρυσὸς δὲ, περισφίγγων τοὺς βαρυτίμους τῶν λίθων, ὁ μέν τις αὐταῖς προμετωπίδιος γίνεται κόσμος, ὁ δὲ περιαυχένιος· καὶ ἄλλος ἐν ζώναις, καὶ ἄλλος τὰς χεῖρας δεσμεῖ καὶ τοὺς πόδας. Χαί ρουσι γὰρ αἱ φιλόχρυσοι δεδεμέναι ταῖς χειροπέδαις, μόνον ἐὰν χρυσὸς ὁ δεσμῶν αὐτὰς ᾖ. Πότε οὖν ψυχῆς ἐπιμελήσεται ὁ γυναικείαις ἐπιθυμίαις ὑπηρετούμενος; Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ ὑπόσαθρα τῶν πολίων καταιγίδες καὶ ζάλαι, οὕτως αἱ πονηραὶ τῶν γυναικῶν διαθέσεις τὰς ἀσθενεῖς ψυχὰς τῶν συνοικούντων καταβαπτίζουσι. Πρὸς τοσαῦτα δὴ οὖν διελκόμενος ὁ πλοῦτος ὑπὸ ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς, ἀλλήλους νικώντων ταῖς ἐφευρέσεσι τῶν ματαίων, εἰκότως οὐδένα καιρὸν ἔχει πρὸς τοὺς ἔξωθεν παρακύπτειν. Ἀλλ' ἐὰν μὲν ἀκούσῃς· Πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, καὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς· ἵνα ἔχῃς ἐφόδια πρὸς τὴν αἰωνίαν ἀπόλαυσιν, ἀπέρχῃ λυπούμενος· ἐὰν δὲ ἀκούσῃς· Δὸς χρήματα γυναιξὶ χλιδώσαις, δὸς λιθοξόοις, τέκτοσι, ψηφοθέ ταις, ζωγράφοις, χαίρεις ὡς δή τι χρημάτων τιμιώτερον κατακτώμενος. Οὐχ ὁρᾷς τοὺς τοίχους τούτους τοὺς ὑπὸ τοῦ χρόνου καταῤῥυέντας, ὧν τὰ λείψανα, ὥσπερ σκόπελοί τινες, διὰ τῆς πόλεως πάσης ἀνέχουσιν; Πόσοι ἦσαν κατὰ τὴν πόλιν πένητες, τούτων ἐγειρομένων, οἳ διὰ τὴν περὶ ταῦτα σπουδὴν ὑπὸ τῶν τότε πλουσίων παρεωρῶντο; Ποῦ τοίνυν ἡ λαμπρὰ τῶν ἔργων κατασκευή; ποῦ δὲ ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ τούτων μεγαλουργίᾳ ζηλούμενος; Οὐ τὰ μὲν συγκέχυται καὶ ἠφάνισται, ὥσπερ τὰ κατὰ παιδιὰν ἐν ταῖς ψάμμοις ὑπὸ τῶν παίδων φιλοτεχνούμενα, ὁ δὲ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ κεῖται, ἐπὶ τῇ σπουδῇ τῶν ματαίων μεταμελόμενος; Μεγάλην ἔχε τὴν ψυχήν· τοῖχοι δὲ καὶ μικροὶ καὶ μείζους τὴν αὐτὴν χρείαν πληροῦσιν. Ὅταν παρέλθω εἰς οἰκίαν ἀνδρὸς ἀπειροκάλου καὶ ὀψιπλούτου, καὶ ἴδω αὐτὴν παντοίοις γεγανωμένην ἄνθεσιν, οἶδα ὅτι οὗτος οὐδὲν τῶν ὁρωμένων τιμιώτερον κέκτηται, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἄψυχα καλλωπίζει, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἀκόσμητον ἔχει. Ποίαν, εἰπέ μοι, χρείαν περισσοτέραν παρέχουσιν ἀργυραῖ κλῖναι καὶ τράπεζαι ἀργυραῖ, ἐλεφάντιναι στιβάδες καὶ ἐλεφάντινοι δίφροι, ὥστε τὸν πλοῦτον διὰ ταῦτα μὴ διαβαίνειν πρὸς τοὺς πτωχοὺς, καίτοι μυρίοι ἐφεστᾶσι τῇ θύρᾳ, πᾶσαν ἐλεεινὴν ἀφιέντες φωνήν; Σὺ δὲ ἀρνῇ τὴν δόσιν, ἀδύνατον εἶναι λέγων ἐπαρκεῖν τοῖς αἰτοῦσι. Καὶ τῇ μὲν γλώσσῃ ἐξόμνυσαι, ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς χειρὸς διελέγχῃ· σιωπῶσα γάρ σου ἡ χεὶρ τὴν ψευδολογίαν κηρύσσει, περιαστραπτομένη ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπὶ τοῦ δακτυλίου σφενδόνης. Πόσους δύναται εἷς σου δακτύλιος χρεῶν ἀπολῦσαι; πόσους οἴκους καταπίπτοντας ἀνορθῶσαι; Μία σου κιβωτὸς τῶν ἱματίων δύναται δῆμον ὅλον ῥιγοῦντα περιβαλεῖν· ἀλλ' ὑπομένεις ἄπρακτον ἀποπέμψαι τὸν πένητα, οὐ φοβούμενος τὸ δίκαιον τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως τοῦ κριτοῦ. Οὐκ ἠλέησας, οὐκ ἐλεηθήσῃ· οὐκ ἤνοιξας τὴν οἰκίαν, ἀποπεμφθήσῃ τῆς βασιλείας· οὐκ ἔδωκας τὸν ἄρτον, οὐ λήψῃ τὴν αἰώνιον ζωήν.
thought_title: The Judge's Questions and the Futility of Luxury
orientation: Basil continues his direct address to the rich, imagining the questions the judge will put to them and then describing how a luxury-loving wife doubles the disease of wealth, leaving no time or wealth for the poor.
pass_a_gloss: What will you answer to the judge, you who clothe the walls, but do not clothe a human being? You who adorn the horses, do you overlook the brother who is unseemly? You who let the grain rot, do you not feed the hungry? You who bury the gold, do you despise the one who is being strangled? And if indeed also a wealth-loving wife lives with you, the disease is double; for she kindles the luxuries; and she increases the pleasures; and she sends goads into the curious desires, devising certain stones, pearls and emeralds and hyacinths, and gold, forging some of it, weaving some of it, and increasing the disease through every lack of taste. For the zeal about these things is not from a side pursuit, but nights and days hold the cares about these things. And countless flatterers, running under their desires, gather the dyers of flowers, the goldsmiths, the perfumers, the weavers, the embroiderers. She gives no time to the husband to breathe because of her continuous commands. No wealth suffices when it is made to serve women's desires, not even if it flows in from rivers; when the barbarian perfume is zealously sought by them, as the oil from the market, and the flowers from the sea, the purple-fish, the pinna, above the wool from the sheep. And gold, binding tight the heavy-priced stones, becomes for them one ornament for the forehead, another for the neck; and another in belts, and another binds the hands and the feet. For the gold-loving women rejoice being bound with handcuffs, only if the thing binding them is gold. When then will he care for the soul, the man who is made to serve women's desires? For just as storms and squalls sink the rotten parts of cities, so the wicked dispositions of women sink the weak souls of those who live with them. Drawn then in so many directions, the wealth by husband and wife, who surpass each other in the inventions of vain things, reasonably has no occasion to look out toward those outside. But if you hear: Sell your possessions, and give to the poor; so that you may have provisions for the eternal enjoyment, you go away grieving; but if you hear: Give money to women who live in luxury, give to stone-cutters, to carpenters, to mosaic-layers, to painters, you rejoice as if acquiring something more precious than money. Do you not see these walls, the ones worn down by time, whose remains, like some crags, rise up through the whole city? How many poor people were in the city, when these were being built, who because of the zeal about these things were overlooked by the rich of that time? Where then is the splendid construction of the works? Where is the one who was envied for the magnificence of these things? Have not the one things been thrown together and destroyed, just as the things crafted in play in the sands by children, and the other lies in Hades, regretting the zeal for vain things? Have a great soul; but walls, both small and larger, fulfill the same need. Whenever I enter the house of a tasteless man and one newly rich, and see it brightened with all kinds of flowers, I know that this man has acquired nothing more precious than the things seen, but he beautifies the lifeless things, and has the soul unadorned. What need, tell me, do silver couches and silver tables provide more abundantly, ivory beds and ivory chairs, so that wealth because of these things does not cross over to the poor, although countless people stand at the door, sending forth every pitiful voice? But you refuse the gift, saying it is impossible to suffice for those who ask. And with the tongue you swear off, but by the hand you are refuted; for your hand, being silent, proclaims the false speech, flashing around by the ring's bezel. How many debtors is one ring of yours able to release? How many falling houses is it able to set upright? One chest of yours of the garments is able to clothe a whole people shivering; but you endure to send away the poor man without effect, not fearing the justice of the repayment of the judge. You did not have mercy, you will not be shown mercy; you did not open the house, you will be sent away from the kingdom; you did not give the bread, you will not receive eternal life.

choices.why: The verb means to put clothing on; keeping 'clothe' preserves the parallel with the unclothed human being.
The participle means being in a shameful or indecent state; 'unseemly' keeps the moral and visual force without modernizing to 'naked'.
The verb is causative of decay; 'let rot' shows the rich man's active neglect of grain while others starve.
The participle is passive and present; 'being strangled' keeps the vivid image of someone perishing from want while gold is buried.
The noun means tastelessness or vulgarity; 'lack of taste' fits Basil's critique of ostentatious luxury.
The noun means supplies for a journey; 'provisions' keeps the metaphor of wealth converted into what carries one to eternal enjoyment.

pass_b_english: What will you answer the judge, you who clothe your walls and do not clothe a human being? You who adorn your horses and overlook your brother in his unseemly state? You who let your grain rot and do not feed the hungry? You who bury your gold and despise the one being strangled? And if a wife who loves wealth lives with you, the disease is doubled. For she kindles your luxuries and increases your love of pleasure, and she sends goads into her fussy desires, devising certain stones—pearls, emeralds, and hyacinths—and gold, working gold in one way, weaving it in another, and through every lack of taste she increases the disease. For the zeal for these things is not a side matter, but nights and days hold the cares about them. And countless flatterers, catering to their desires, gather the dyers of bright colors, the goldsmiths, the perfumers, the weavers, the embroiderers. She gives the man no time to breathe because of her continuous commands. No wealth suffices when it serves women's desires, not even if it flows in from rivers—when they eagerly seek barbarian perfume as if it were oil from the market, and the dyes from the sea, the murex, the pinna, above the wool from sheep. And gold, binding the precious stones, becomes for them one ornament for the forehead, another for the neck; and another is in belts, and another binds their hands and feet. For women who love gold rejoice to be bound with manacles, if only the thing binding them is gold. When then will the man who serves women's desires care for his soul? For just as storms and squalls sink the rotten ships, so the wicked dispositions of women sink the weak souls of those who live with them. Wealth, then, being dragged in so many directions by man and wife, who outdo each other in the inventions of vain things, naturally has no opportunity to look out toward those outside. But if you hear, 'Sell your possessions and give to the poor' (Matthew 19:21), so that you may have provisions for eternal enjoyment, you go away grieving. But if you hear, 'Give money to women who live in luxury, give to stonecutters, carpenters, mosaicists, painters,' you rejoice as if you were acquiring something more precious than money. Do you not see these walls, worn down by time, whose remains stand up through the whole city like crags? How many poor people were in the city when these were being built, who were overlooked by the rich of that time because of their zeal for these things? Where then is the splendid construction of the works? Where is the man admired for the magnificence of these things? Have not the works been thrown into confusion and obliterated, like things crafted in sand by children at play, while the man lies in Hades, regretting his zeal for vain things? What a great soul you have; walls both small and larger fulfill the same need. When I enter the house of a man of no taste and newly acquired wealth, and I see it decked out with all kinds of colors, I know that this man has acquired nothing more precious than the things seen, but he beautifies lifeless things and keeps his soul unadorned. Tell me, what greater need do silver couches and silver tables provide, ivory beds and ivory chairs, so that wealth should not pass over to the poor because of these things—even though countless poor stand at the door, sending forth every pitiable cry? But you refuse the gift, saying it is impossible to help those who ask. And with your tongue you swear falsely, but by your hand you are refuted; for your silent hand proclaims your falsehood, flashing with the ring on your finger. How many debtors can one ring of yours release? How many falling houses can it raise up? One chest of your garments can clothe a whole people shivering with cold; but you endure sending the poor man away empty-handed, not fearing the justice of the judge's recompense. You did not show mercy; you will not be shown mercy. You did not open your house; you will be sent away from the kingdom. You did not give bread; you will not receive eternal life.

problems.quote: you who bury your gold and despise the one being strangled
problems.source_quote: ὁ τὸν χρυσὸν κατορύσσων, τοῦ ἀγχομένου καταφρονεῖς
problems.why: ἀγχομένου means 'one being choked/drowned' (by poverty), not 'strangled' as violence.
problems.fix: you who bury your gold and despise the one being choked by need

problems.why: περιέργοις means 'meddlesome/busybody' or 'fussy', not 'idle'; the desires are overactive, not idle.
problems.ruling: περιέργοις means meddlesome/busybody, not 'idle'; desires are overactive not idle.

problems.quote: women who love gold rejoice to be bound in handcuffs
problems.why: χειροπέδαις are bracelets/armlets, not 'handcuffs' (which implies punishment/restraint).
problems.fix: women who love gold rejoice to be bound with bracelets
problems.ruling: χειροπέδαις are bracelets/armlets here, not 'handcuffs'; wordplay on bonds/decorative gold.

problems.quote: you who bury your gold and despise the one being strangled
problems.source_quote: ὁ τὸν χρυσὸν κατορύσσων, τοῦ ἀγχομένου καταφρονεῖς
problems.why: ἀγχομένου means 'the one choking/starving', not 'being strangled'; context is hunger, not violence.
problems.fix: you who bury your gold and despise the one who is starving

problems.quote: she sends goads into your fussy desires
problems.why: ταῖς περιέργοις ἐπιθυμίαις is dative; she sends goads 'into' or 'for' her own fussy desires, not 'your' desires.
problems.fix: she sends goads into her fussy desires
problems.ruling: ταῖς περιέργοις ἐπιθυμίαις are her own desires; 'your' wrongly shifts reference to the husband.

problems.quote: some of it forged, some of it woven
problems.source_quote: τὸν μὲν χαλκεύουσα, τὸν δὲ ἐξυφαίνουσα
problems.why: The participles are feminine singular (she forges, she weaves); subject is the wife, not 'some...some' of gold.
problems.fix: she forges the one and weaves the other
problems.ruling: χαλκεύουσα/ἐξυφαίνουσα are feminine participles: 'she forges, she weaves'; not 'some of gold'.

problems.quote: And with your tongue you swear falsely
problems.why: ἐξόμνυσαι means 'you swear' or 'you take an oath', not specifically 'swear falsely'; the falsehood is revealed by context, not the verb itself.
problems.fix: And with your tongue you swear an oath
problems.ruling: ἐξόμνυσαι means 'you swear' not 'swear falsely'; adding 'falsely' over-translates, though context implies it.

problems.why: Subject is wife, not gold; she works gold and weaves gold (into fabric), not 'the one...the other.'
problems.fix: working gold in one way, weaving it in another

problems.why: ὑποτρέχοντες means 'catering to' or 'fawning upon,' not 'running under.'
problems.ruling: ὑποτρέχοντες means 'catering to/fawning upon'; 'running under' is literal, misleading English.

problems.quote: the flowers of the sea, the purple shell, the pinna
problems.source_quote: τὰ δὲ ἐκ θαλάττης ἄνθη, ἡ κόχλος, ἡ πίννα
problems.why: ἄνθη here means 'dyes' or 'colors,' not flowers; κόχλος is purple-fish/murex, not 'shell.'
problems.fix: the dyes from the sea, the murex, the pinna
problems.ruling: ἄνθη = 'dyes/colors' here; κόχλος = murex/purple-fish; 'flowers, shell' misleads readers on luxury trade.

problems.quote: women who love gold rejoice to be bound with bracelets
problems.why: χειροπέδαις are manacles/fetters, not bracelets; deliberate irony of bondage lost.
problems.fix: women who love gold rejoice to be bound with manacles
problems.ruling: χειροπέδαις = 'fetters/manacles'; 'bracelets' loses deliberate irony of gold as bondage.

problems.why: Imperative is sarcastic/rhetorical: 'You have a great soul!' (ironic), not encouragement.
problems.fix: What a great soul you have!
problems.ruling: Μεγάλην ἔχε τὴν ψυχήν is ironic rebuke; imperative 'Have a great soul' misleads as encouragement.

problems.quote: gleaming with all kinds of flowers
problems.why: ἄνθη here means 'colors/patterns,' not flowers; context is interior decoration.
problems.fix: decked out with all kinds of colors
problems.ruling: ἄνθη = 'colors/patterns' in interior décor context; 'flowers' misleads readers about decoration.

problems.quote: with your tongue you swear an oath
problems.why: ἐξόμνυσαι means 'deny on oath' or 'swear falsely,' not merely 'swear an oath'; perjury is key.
problems.fix: with your tongue you swear falsely
problems.ruling: ἐξόμνυσαι = 'swear falsely/deny on oath'; 'swear an oath' omits perjury, key to contrast with hand.

fixed.note: πολίων is a slip for πλοίων: storms and squalls sink rotten ships, not parts of cities; the checker's 'foundations' is wrong, and so is its objection to 'sink' (καταβαπτίζω means to sink).

dismissed.quote: she sends goads into her fussy desires
dismissed.why: Subject and object reversed: wife inserts goads into desires, not sends goads into desires.
dismissed.note: The wife is the subject in both the Greek and the English, so the claimed reversal does not exist; 'sends goads into' is a fair rendering of ἐνίησι.

dismissed.quote: the dyes from the sea, the murex, the pinna, above the wool from sheep
dismissed.why: ὑπὲρ means 'more than,' not 'above'; they value sea-dyes more than wool.
dismissed.note: After 'eagerly seek', 'above the wool' already means 'more than', so the English says what ὑπὲρ says.

dismissed.quote: working gold in one way, weaving it in another
dismissed.why: τὸν refers back to λίθους (stones), not gold; she works some stones, weaves others into fabric.
dismissed.note: τὸν μὲν / τὸν δὲ are masculine singular and point back to χρυσὸν right before them, not to the plural λίθους; forged gold and gold thread is correct.

dismissed.quote: barbarian perfume as if it were oil from the market
dismissed.why: Wrong comparison: they seek barbarian perfume as eagerly as they seek common oil from market, not 'as if it were oil.'
dismissed.note: 'As if it were oil from the market' fairly gives the point that they treat costly foreign perfume like a common staple.

dismissed.quote: decked out with all kinds of colors
dismissed.why: ἄνθεσιν here means floral decorations/patterns, not colors; 'decked with flowers' or 'floral designs.'
dismissed.note: ἄνθη often means bright colours or dyes, so 'all kinds of colors' is a fair rendering for a decorated house.

dismissed.quote: with your tongue you swear falsely
dismissed.why: ἐξόμνυσαι means 'you swear off/renounce' (deny obligation), not 'swear falsely' (perjury).
dismissed.note: ἐξόμνυσαι is a denial on oath that the next clause calls a lie (ψευδολογία), so 'swear falsely' is fair.
